chrome.changelogLead: What changed in each release, written for the people using it. Every version's complete notes and downloads live on GitHub.

home.metaTitle: ReadAware — Free, Open-Source Ebook Reader That's Aware of You
home.metaDescription: A free, open-source ebook reader for Windows, macOS, Linux, and Android. One reader for EPUB, MOBI, AZW3, FB2, CBZ, CBR, TXT, HTML, and PDF that builds memory from your reading, grows through plugins, and syncs end-to-end encrypted — local-first and private.
home.heroLead: A free, open-source ebook reader. Read your own files offline, then add context-aware AI and encrypted sync when you need them.
home.shelfAlt: The ReadAware library — a grid of book covers across many languages and formats.
home.shelfCaption: Your library — every format in one place.
home.readerTitle: A calm place to read anything
home.readerBody: Import a file and start reading. There is no conversion and no cloud upload; your highlights, notes, and place in the book stay with the original text. When you want more focus, read sentence by sentence — the page holds back, a floating strip steps you through, and read-aloud can follow along.
home.readerAlt: A page of Pride and Prejudice in the ReadAware reader, one sentence held in focus while the rest of the page recedes.
home.readerCaption: Reading Pride and Prejudice one sentence at a time.
home.memoryTitle: It's aware of what you've read
home.memoryBody: Ask about a passage, a book, or your whole shelf. ReadAware answers from your own reading — the line you marked three books ago, the question you asked last week, the thread that runs through everything on your shelf. It doesn't replay a chat history; it keeps a durable memory of what matters and brings it back at the moment it's relevant.
home.contextAlt: The ReadAware assistant surveying the reader's shelf and recent reading, and naming the thread that runs through it.
home.contextCaption: The assistant, answering from your own shelf.
home.pluginBody: Sandboxed plugins from the built-in marketplace add read-aloud voices, dictionaries, reading themes, feeds that read like books. And they reach deeper than features: a plugin can hand the assistant a new tool, and it simply starts using it. The reader doesn't just gain buttons — it learns new skills.
home.pluginAlt: The ReadAware plugin panel — dictionary, themes, and RSS reader installed, each in its own sandbox, some handing the assistant new tools.
home.pluginCaption: Voices, dictionaries, themes, feeds — and tools the assistant picks up.
home.syncBody: Optional end-to-end encrypted sync carries books, highlights, notes, reading position, and memory between devices. Free accounts include 50 MB; paid plans expand storage. The sync relay stores ciphertext. Available on desktop, Android, and iOS.

notes.title: One engine, every format
notes.body: EPUB, MOBI, AZW3, FB2, CBZ, CBR, TXT, HTML, and PDF open in the same reader, with the same selection, highlights, and progress. Nothing is converted; the original file is what you keep.

notes.title: Aware, not archival
notes.body: Reading becomes memory the app can act on. ReadAware keeps what matters and surfaces it when it's relevant — it's there in the moment, not filed away.

notes.title: Plugins teach it new skills
notes.body: Marketplace plugins add voices, dictionaries, themes, and feeds — and hand the assistant tools it picks up and uses.

notes.title: Open source, local-first, encrypted sync
notes.body: The code is public under AGPL-3.0. Your library and memory are stored locally; optional sync is end-to-end encrypted. AI sends relevant context to your chosen model provider.

download.title: Get ReadAware
download.intro: Free offline reading, highlights, and notes. Optional plans expand sync and add built-in AI; your own API key works without a ReadAware AI subscription, with provider charges separate.
download.signingNote: macOS builds are signed and notarized. Windows builds are not yet code-signed and may show a SmartScreen warning. Download only from the official release.

pricing.metaDescription: The reader is free, including local books, annotations, and BYOK AI. Free accounts include 50 MB of encrypted sync. Paid plans expand storage; Pro and Max also include built-in AI.
pricing.title: Pricing
pricing.lead: The reader is free, including local books, annotations, and BYOK AI. Free accounts include 50 MB of encrypted sync. Paid plans expand storage; Pro and Max also include built-in AI.
pricing.purchaseSuccess: Payment received — your plan is active. Sign in to the app with the email you used at checkout.
pricing.checkoutFailed: Couldn't start checkout. Try again, or write to us.
pricing.finePrintTitle: The fine print, in plain words
finePrint: AI credits: 1 credit = $0.001 of model usage at list price. A typical question costs 2–4 credits, so 5,000 credits is roughly a thousand conversations. Credits reset monthly.
ReadAware charges no AI subscription fee for using your own key on any plan. Your model provider may charge for API usage.
Synced data is end-to-end encrypted. The server stores ciphertext it cannot read; the passphrase never leaves your devices.
Built-in AI requests pass through our relay to the model provider over TLS and are never logged or stored — only token counts are metered. If that trade-off isn't for you, use your own key.
Downgrading never deletes anything. Over-quota accounts keep reading and downloading their data; only new uploads pause.

plans.tagline: The whole reading app, no account needed.

AI chat and memory with your own API key
All data local, on your disk
50 MB encrypted sync to try multi-device

changelog.metaDescription: What changed in each ReadAware release, written for the people using it.

entries.summary: This Cambria release adds a customizable reader header and footer, advanced typography, a searchable font picker and Xiaomi MiMo read-aloud voices.

items.title: Reader header and footer
items.body: Show the chapter, book title, progress, page numbers, time and battery in thin strips above and below the page, and arrange them by dragging in Settings → Customize. They are on by default on Android and iOS, where the reader hides the system status bar.

items.title: Advanced typography
items.body: Set exact values for font size, line height, paragraph spacing, margins and weight instead of preset steps. First-line indent can follow the book, be turned off or be set yourself.

items.title: Searchable font picker
items.body: Curated, plugin, imported and installed fonts share one list with section headings, and you can search it by name.

items.title: Xiaomi MiMo read-aloud voices
items.body: Xiaomi MiMo is available as a text-to-speech provider for reading aloud.

items.title: More text per page on phones
items.body: The safe area around the notch and home indicator counts toward the page margins, so iPhones no longer lose about three lines per page.

items.title: No font flash between chapters
items.body: A new chapter appears only after its font has loaded instead of briefly showing a fallback font.

items.title: Exports on iOS
items.body: Exporting files on iPhone and iPad no longer produces empty files or fails.

items.title: Older iOS and Safari versions
items.body: The app and EPUB loading work on iOS 16.0 to 16.3. The minimum supported iOS version is now 16.0.

items.title: Inline glyph images stay in the sentence
items.body: Small images used as substitute characters in CJK books stay on their line of text.

entries.summary: This Cambria release adds image backgrounds for reading, tap zones and volume keys for turning pages, whole-folder import and your own font files on every platform.

items.title: Image backgrounds for reading
items.body: The built-in Image Background plugin turns a local PNG, JPEG or WebP into a reading theme. Preview the image, choose a base theme for colors and typography, and set its opacity and dimming. You can switch between image themes and regular page colors right from the plugin page.

items.title: Tap zones and volume keys turn pages
items.body: Settings → Reading → Page Turning adds tapping the sides of the page, or a one-handed forward zone, and on Android the volume keys. Both are off by default, and the Agent can change them for you.

items.title: Import a whole folder
items.body: Add every book in a folder at once on desktop, Android and iOS, or drop a folder onto the window on desktop. Each book remembers its folder, so you can ask the Agent to group your shelf by it.

items.title: Your own fonts on every platform
items.body: Import TTF, OTF, WOFF, WOFF2 or TTC files from the reading font menu on desktop, Android and iOS. Imported fonts sync to your other devices.

items.title: One dropdown for reading fonts
items.body: Importing and removing fonts happens inside the font dropdown instead of a separate list below it.

items.title: Sentence mode follows your other devices
items.body: After a sync, sentence and paragraph mode resume where you stopped reading on the other device instead of jumping back to an old chapter.

items.title: Swipe back in iOS Settings
items.body: The edge-swipe gesture goes back a level in Settings on iPhone and iPad.

entries.summary: This Cambria patch makes page turns on touch screens respond to a short swipe, stops the app from zooming like a web page, and keeps the AI model list open on Android.

items.title: Short swipes turn the page
items.body: In page-turn mode on phones and tablets, a quick flick turns the page even when your finger slows before lifting, and a slower drag turns it once it covers a quarter of the page. A swipe always moves exactly one page.

items.title: No more zooming the whole app
items.body: A two-finger pinch or a double tap no longer magnifies the entire app on Android and iOS. PDFs and comics still zoom with a pinch, and text size stays in the reader's font settings.

items.title: The model list stays open on Android
items.body: In Settings → AI, the model picker no longer closes as soon as the on-screen keyboard appears; the field moves above the keyboard so you can search and choose.

entries.summary: This Cambria patch keeps marketplace plugins up to date on their own, explains why a plugin isn't running and how to fix it, and makes citations in AI replies work.

items.title: Plugins that update themselves
items.body: Plugins you install or update from the marketplace now stay current on their own, checked daily and right after ReadAware updates. They keep their book access and on/off state, and a plugin you turned off is updated without running. Updates asking for new permissions wait for your approval in Settings → Plugins, and plugins installed from a folder or zip are never replaced. Plugins installed before 0.6.6 announce their next update once; update them from the marketplace and they update automatically after that.

items.title: A plugin that can't run says why
items.body: Instead of pointing you to the log, the plugin's row explains whether it was built for an older ReadAware or needs a newer one, with an Update button when the marketplace has a compatible release, or a shortcut to check for app updates.

items.title: Plugin number settings stay in range
items.body: A plugin's settings page refuses a number outside the range the plugin declares and says which values it accepts.

items.title: Sync waits as long as the server asks
items.body: When the sync server is busy, the next attempt happens at the time it requests instead of after a ten-minute backoff.

items.title: A plugin kit for people and coding agents
items.body: The plugin repository's template, typings and checks now match this release, a single guide walks a coding agent through building a plugin, and the API reference lists every capability and method with the version this release ships.

items.title: Footnote citations in AI replies
items.body: Clicking a footnote marker jumps to its note within the reply, and the arrow jumps back, instead of opening an external-link prompt.

items.title: Links in Chinese and Japanese replies
items.body: A bare web address followed by punctuation such as a full-width closing parenthesis no longer pulls that punctuation and the following text into the link.

entries.summary: This Cambria patch lets you zoom into PDF and comic pages, lock a zoomed view while you turn pages, and rebuilds the contents of books that barely have one.

items.title: Zoom for PDFs and comics
items.body: Pinch on the trackpad or touch screen, or press ⌘= and ⌘− (Ctrl on Windows and Linux). The spot under your fingers stays put, and a zoomed page scrolls in every direction. Reading appearance lets you choose whether 100% fits the page's width or the whole page.

items.title: One click back to the fit
items.body: The percentage shows while you zoom, and while the reader's controls are up a zoomed page keeps it on screen with a button back to 100%. ⌘0 does the same.

items.title: Lock a zoomed view
items.body: In single- and two-page modes, lock the view from the zoom indicator or with ⌘L. The wheel, arrow keys and swipes turn pages again, and every page opens on the same part — one column of a research paper, page after page.

items.title: Contents for books that barely have one
items.body: Book sets whose contents list only their volumes, and PDFs without an outline, get a nested contents list recovered from their headings.

items.title: Your place on a zoomed page
items.body: Each book remembers its zoom and where on the page you were reading, so it reopens on the same passage.

items.title: Sharp at any zoom
items.body: Past the render budget, the part of a PDF page on screen is drawn again at full resolution.

items.title: Chapter summaries that follow the real chapters
items.body: Chapters are worked out once for the reader and the assistant, so multi-part books and book sets are summarized chapter by chapter.

items.title: Large Kindle books
items.body: Big or slightly damaged KF8/AZW3 files open reliably, and jumps inside them take milliseconds instead of seconds.

items.title: Publisher layouts stay in the column
items.body: Covers, code, wide tables and positioned blocks no longer render blank or spill onto the next page.

items.title: Missing covers
items.body: EPUB covers named by file path now appear, and a cover that never reached this device is taken again from the book file.

items.title: Progress bar jumps
items.body: Jumping with the progress bar while a chapter change is still animating no longer gets lost.

items.title: Old backups
items.body: Backups now use the encrypted archive only; an old v1 JSON backup is recognized and explained instead of reported as a wrong password.

entries.summary: This Cambria patch moves the reader's controls within reach of your thumb on a phone, lets panels swipe away, and opens books faster on iPhone.

items.title: Phone reader controls at the bottom
items.body: On a phone, contents, notes, reading mode, appearance and chat sit in a toolbar at the bottom of the screen, while the top bar keeps back, the title and More. Arrange the toolbar in Settings → Customize, separately from the desktop header.

items.title: Appearance and notes open from the bottom bar
items.body: The bar grows upward to hold them instead of a card floating over the page; pull it down to close it. Appearance leads with text size and page colors, with fonts and finer typography one tap away.

items.title: Swipe panels away
items.body: Contents and chat close with the back swipe from the left edge, or by dragging them out the way they came. A note swipes left to delete it.

items.title: Faster book opening on iPhone
items.body: Large books open markedly faster; a long biography went from about 1.3 seconds to 0.5 on an iPhone 14 Pro.

items.title: Controls that appear at once
items.body: A tap on the page no longer waits a quarter second before showing the reader's controls.

items.title: Notes that are easier to scan
items.body: The notes list uses the app's own type rather than the book's, with each highlight's color beside its passage.

items.title: Status bar on iPhone
items.body: The status bar hides while reading again.

items.title: Damaged MOBI files
items.body: A damaged MOBI file is reported as a damaged copy instead of as DRM-protected.

entries.summary: This Cambria patch starts ReadAware again on e-readers with an older browser engine, and reopens books where you last read, including after turning back.

items.title: Could not start on some Android e-readers
items.body: Devices whose system web engine dates from before late 2023, such as many e-ink readers without Google Play, have stopped at a "Could not start" screen since 0.6.0. The app now fills in the engine features it relies on itself, and that screen names the engine version so a report can be acted on.

items.title: Books reopening at a page you had left
items.body: Since 0.6.0 the app kept the furthest page you had reached and ignored turning back, so closing a book after going back to an earlier page reopened it at the later one. A book now reopens where you last were, on every device, and existing progress is corrected from your reading history on first launch.

entries.summary: This Cambria patch gives Sentence Reader a hold menu on phones, draws your marks the moment you make them, repairs broken tables of contents on open, and brings back the end-of-book screen.

items.title: A hold menu for Sentence Reader on phones
items.body: The bottom toolbar is gone on phones and tablets. Press and hold anywhere on the page to open the current sentence's actions under your finger: highlight, underline, note, ask AI, copy and read aloud. Slide onto an action and lift to run it, or lift in place and tap. Navigation, the sentence and paragraph switch, plugin lookups, the panels and exit sit behind More. Tapping the highlighted sentence opens the same menu.

items.title: Marks appear instantly
items.body: A new highlight or underline is drawn as soon as it is saved instead of up to a second later, and books with many marks no longer repaint all of them for each new one.

items.title: Tables of contents that aimed every chapter at the cover
items.body: Some converted books list every chapter but point them all at the first page, so navigation landed on the cover, the chapter label was wrong and continuous scroll treated the whole book as one chapter. The reader now relocates those entries to the chapters that open with their titles.

items.title: The end-of-book screen is reachable again
items.body: Turning past the last page did nothing on desktop or phones. Keyboard, wheel, tap and swipe now all finish the book.

items.title: Sentence actions on touch
items.body: Tapping the highlighted sentence opens its actions again; the previous release stepped to the next sentence instead.

items.title: AI providers on custom ports
items.body: HTTP provider addresses with a non-default port are accepted.

entries.summary: This Cambria update opens large books instantly in continuous scroll, makes Sentence Reader dependable on phones, and lets Beta channel devices find updates anywhere.

items.title: Read on from the page you turned to
items.body: In paginated layouts, after you flip pages by hand, the next tap or volume-key step in Sentence Reader continues from the page you are looking at. The sentence you left stays one tap away behind Back to current sentence.

items.title: A go-to box in Jumper
items.body: One field answers with chapters, printed pages, and a live text search of the book, with the table of contents and your current chapter underneath. Plugins can now offer their own search in list views.

items.title: Web search on by default
items.body: Add your search provider's API key to use web search with the assistant. The update dialog offers a shortcut to AI settings when the key is missing and respects an existing choice to keep search off.

items.title: Instant opening in continuous scroll
items.body: Books whose chapters span dozens of files used to take seconds to open or jump. The reader now shows the target page at once and keeps only the files around your position loaded, without moving the text under you.

items.title: Fast search in long books
items.body: Case- and accent-insensitive text search now folds each section once, so a full-book query that took minutes completes in under a second.

items.title: Sentences split the way a reader expects
items.body: Opening quotes start the line of dialogue they open, abbreviations such as Mr., Dr., and e.g. no longer end a sentence, and footnote numbers no longer fuse two sentences together.

items.title: Steadier sentence stepping on phones
items.body: The viewport stays put while you step through visible text, sentences that span a page boundary are revealed before advancing, and tapping the highlighted sentence keeps advancing. The compact toolbar keeps annotation actions and exit on one row.

items.title: A Beta channel that works everywhere
items.body: Beta updates are found through a fixed release pointer instead of the GitHub API, so devices on shared networks or where the API is blocked now see new betas.

items.title: Fewer blank screens when opening large books
items.body: Reading positions restore even when the saved location has no visible rectangle, PDF pages wait for layout before restoring, and chapter jumps in scroll mode no longer leave the previous chapter on screen.

items.title: Sentence Reader controls on Android
items.body: Volume keys work again while a note or chat field has focus, and a dragged toolbar can no longer be parked under the status bar or the gesture strip.

items.title: Phone sheets stay out of the way
items.body: The table of contents and chat sheets close when the reader chrome hides and no longer reappear over the page when a book is reopened.

items.title: Two plugins retired
items.body: The Reading Goals and Annotations plugins are removed. The reader handles annotations natively, and the assistant carries reading intent without a plugin.

entries.summary: Cambria keeps your furthest reading progress across devices, brings web sources and images into the assistant, and makes your library easier to back up and use with other tools.

items.title: Web research with your own keys
items.body: Connect TinyFish, Exa, Tavily, SerpAPI, or Brave for web search and retrieval. The assistant stays with your selected provider, links to sources, and can show relevant images. Models that support vision can also inspect image content.

items.title: Encrypted backups of your reading workspace
items.body: Create a full encrypted backup of your books, annotations, conversations, memory, settings, and plugin data. Review what will be restored before merging it into another installation, while keeping that device's account session and local settings.

items.title: Your library in other assistants
items.body: An optional, token-protected local HTTP API lets other tools read your library and reading context. Copy the ReadAware skill installation prompt from Settings to connect a compatible assistant.

items.title: A more useful reading assistant
items.body: Retry a failed model step without starting the conversation over, and expand one grouped view to inspect tool activity. Fiction retains reading-progress spoiler protection, while history and biography can use relevant factual context.

items.title: A reader that remembers your preferences
items.body: Font choices are remembered by book language, two-page layouts have more room, and chapter navigation follows the table of contents even when several chapters share one source file.

items.title: More capable plugins
items.body: Plugins can work with more of your reading workspace through scoped permissions. Updated navigation, annotations, and reading goals make their everyday controls simpler, while plugin sync transports have their own settings and a manual Sync now action.

items.title: Help shape ReadAware
items.body: The update dialog now offers a direct way to star ReadAware on GitHub or join the Discord community. About includes a small credit to AHpx at the bottom.

items.title: Offline progress no longer moves backward
items.body: Sync keeps the furthest reading position across devices. If an offline device has reached page 300 and another device has a newer record at page 200, reconnecting keeps page 300. Reading time is handled separately from reading position.

items.title: More accurate reading time and smoother navigation
items.body: Reading sessions pause while the app is idle or in the background. Touch annotations respond more reliably, and chapter transitions in scroll mode no longer drift into the wrong section.

entries.summary: ReadAware remembers your desktop window, imports books more reliably on Android, and brings you back to the right passage when you resume reading.

items.title: Your window stays yours
items.body: The desktop app remembers its size, position, and maximized or fullscreen state when you close it. Returning from maximized keeps your previous window size and position, and disconnecting a monitor no longer leaves the window out of reach. These settings stay on each device.

items.title: More reliable Android imports
items.body: Books picked through Android's file picker now pass through the app's private cache, avoiding import failures caused by unavailable or unwritable external cache folders.

items.title: EPUBs on older Android WebViews
items.body: EPUB metadata no longer depends on newer browser functions that some Android WebViews lack, fixing failures when importing or opening books on those devices.

items.title: Return to the right passage
items.body: Saved reading positions and passage links return you to the intended passage in scroll mode. Forward and backward navigation also moves by the reader's visible height instead of a single pixel.

entries.summary: Importing gets instant and covers stop hiding. Books land on the shelf with their cover in a fraction of a second, covers now reach your other devices without opening anything, Kindle-format books open cleanly again, and macOS builds are signed and notarized.

items.title: Signed and notarized on macOS
items.body: ReadAware for macOS is now signed with a Developer ID and notarized by Apple, so it opens on first launch like any other app — no Open Anyway, no Terminal workaround.

items.title: A cover for every book
items.body: A book that declares no cover now shows its first in-book illustration on the shelf — EPUB, MOBI, AZW3 and FB2 alike — so files from converters and scans stop landing as blank tiles.

items.title: Delete your account in the app
items.body: Settings → Data & Sync can delete your sync account outright. The relay cancels any billing and erases everything it held for you.

items.title: Import in a blink
items.body: Picking a book copies it, checks for duplicates by content, reads its metadata and files its cover in one native step; a 36 MB EPUB reaches the shelf in about a tenth of a second, with its real title, author and cover already in place. Importing a book you already have is recognized even under a different file name and copies nothing.

items.title: PDF covers and titles on every platform
items.body: Windows, Linux, iOS and Android render a PDF's cover right after import instead of waiting for you to open it, and PDF titles and authors are read from the document everywhere.

items.title: Covers follow your books across devices
items.body: Synced books used to sit coverless until you opened them. Covers now travel ahead of the book file, and each device keeps fetching the ones it is missing after every sync, repainting the tile the moment one arrives.

items.title: A lighter shelf
items.body: Cover artwork no longer rides inside the library data; each tile loads its cover straight from local storage, so large libraries open faster and use far less memory.

items.title: Chapter marks for Kindle books
items.body: The progress bar now shows chapter boundaries for MOBI and AZW3 books too.

items.title: MOBI and AZW3 books open without errors
items.body: The contents repair mistook every Kindle-format book for one without a usable table of contents and filled it with entries the reader could not resolve, raising an error per chapter the moment the book opened.

items.title: Switching books inside the reader
items.body: Opening another file while a book is open no longer throws layout errors from the book being closed.

items.title: Old-style EPUB covers
items.body: A cover page listed in the guide, or a cover entry pointing at an image path instead of an id, is now found at import instead of showing a placeholder until first open.

entries.summary: Sync goes self-hosted and PDFs grow up. A new WebDAV plugin syncs your encrypted library through your own server; PDFs open in about a second, scroll as one continuous document, and select text precisely; and the shelf learns drag and drop.

items.title: Sync through your own server
items.body: The new WebDAV Sync plugin turns any WebDAV host — Nextcloud, 坚果云, and friends — into a sync backend. Your library is end-to-end encrypted before it leaves the device, so the server only ever stores sealed data it cannot read; connect each device with the same server and passphrase and everything converges, books included.

items.title: Sync backends as plugins
items.body: Plugin developers get a new sync:transport capability: the app keeps encryption, the event log, and merge, while a plugin only carries sealed data to the remote of its choosing. WebDAV is the first tenant.

items.title: PDFs scroll like PDFs
items.body: Scroll mode for PDFs and comics is now one continuous document: the scrollbar spans every page, jumps land anywhere instantly, and pages flow past without swapping screens. Scroll is now the default for these books, and their layout choice is remembered separately, so paging through a novel and scrolling a paper no longer fight over one setting.

items.title: Drag and drop on the shelf
items.body: Books drag straight onto a collection, and while you drag, a dock appears with every collection plus new collection and remove as drop zones. Dragging a selected book carries the whole selection along.

Big PDFs open in about a second. A large scanned book could take half a minute before its first page appeared and stall again on its outline; the reader now fetches only the bytes the visible page needs.
Page turns in single and double-page modes are instant: nearby pages render ahead of you and recently read ones stay warm. Short documents stay fully rendered.
Selecting text in a PDF no longer glitches when the drag starts a little off the letters — the selection follows your pointer the way it should.
Plugin network access broke in 0.5.0 — RSS feed refresh and text-to-speech failed with a permissions error no permission could fix. Both work again.
PDFs imported while the window was covered or in another Space ended up coverless until first opened; covers now render regardless.
Dragging a book inside the shelf no longer summons the drop-to-import overlay.

entries.summary: Your library learns to travel. End-to-end encrypted sync carries books, progress, annotations, and AI conversations across devices; the book memory builds while you read; and every error in the app now speaks like a person.

items.title: Sync across devices
items.body: Sign in with Google or GitHub, set a passphrase, and your books, reading positions, highlights, notes, AI conversations, and covers follow you — end-to-end encrypted, so the server only ever sees ciphertext. Changes arrive live, big books travel in resumable chunks, and a per-book panel shows exactly what has reached the cloud.

items.title: Settings that roam
items.body: Themes, typography, AI provider settings, and API keys travel with your account. A fresh install feels like your own within a minute of signing in.

items.title: A book memory that keeps up
items.body: The character and concept graph now builds in the first minutes after you open a book instead of over hours of idle time. The assistant queries it on demand, tells narrative books from expository ones, merges character nicknames, and mines your older conversations for memories instead of forgetting them.

items.title: Two update channels
items.body: Choose Stable or Beta in Settings → About, and a What's New dialog walks you through each upgrade.

items.title: Crash follow-up
items.body: If ReadAware crashes, the next launch offers to send a diagnostics report — with a preview, and never without your confirmation.

Every error in the app was rebuilt to speak plainly: localized, actionable messages instead of raw error dumps, retry offered only when retrying can help, and a direct link to the fix when one exists.
The OpenRouter model picker now searches the full catalog with pricing shown inline, and Ollama Cloud joins the provider list.
Plugin updates stage with automatic rollback, and plugins can now ship their own app and reader themes.
Scanned PDFs get their text extracted, so the assistant can finally read them. Page turns work from the mouse wheel in paginated mode.
Android can finally import TXT files — the system picker's type filter predated TXT support and greyed them out. TXT files also offer ReadAware in "Open with" on every platform.
Importing the same book twice now recognizes the duplicate and keeps one copy.

entries.summary: A patch that opens the front door: book files open straight from your file manager, drag-and-drop imports, and every illustration gets a full-screen viewer.

items.title: Open with ReadAware
items.body: Make ReadAware the default app for your book files and double-clicking one lands directly in the reader, with the book added to your shelf on the way. If the app is already running, the existing window takes over — no second copy.

items.title: Drop books to import
items.body: Drag book files anywhere onto the window and they import on the spot.

items.title: A closer look at illustrations
items.body: Tap an image in any book to view it full screen. Zoom around the cursor with the wheel or a pinch, drag to pan, double-click to toggle fit, and a small toolbar covers zoom, rotation, copying to the clipboard, and closing.

entries.summary: A patch for the statistics page and the sentence reader: charts you can tap, and a plugin that finally keeps its settings — plus a progress readout and a session timer — under its own roof.

items.title: Tap the charts
items.body: The reading-stats bars now hand the ink highlight to whichever bar you tap — daily, weekday, and time-of-day charts alike — and it stays where you put it.

items.title: The sentence reader keeps its own settings
items.body: Step unit, tap to advance, and swipe to step moved into the plugin's own settings page, joined by two new options: a chapter position readout (12 / 87) and a session timer that restarts on every entry and is never saved. Both live on a small floating chip you can drag anywhere.
Chart tooltips traded their floating card for a quiet ink label pinned above the bars.
The About page shows the series codename beside the version.
The Total time headline no longer overflows on phones, and tapping a chart no longer draws a focus ring.
Turning the readouts off in settings applies without restarting the app.
iOS no longer shows two selection menus at once in the reader.

entries.summary: The first release of the El Alto series, and a release about distance: the actions you need while reading moved onto the sentence itself, the panels worth opening moved one tap away, and the assistant stopped taking detours before answering.

items.title: Tap the sentence
items.body: In sentence or paragraph reading, tapping the highlighted sentence opens its actions right there — copy, highlight, underline, note, ask AI, dictionary — instead of a reach for the bottom bar.

items.title: Doors instead of a toolbar
items.body: The floating navigator strip opens the table of contents, your notes, reading appearance, or chat in one tap, and pages itself on phones so it always fits one row.

items.title: Updates introduce themselves
items.body: After the app updates, a quiet link opens this changelog in your language. Dismiss it, or let it fade on its own after two days.

The reading assistant answers in the language you write in, reports reading time in hours and minutes rather than raw counters, and no longer inventories your stats before answering a question about the book.
Spoiler protection now also fences what the assistant may already know about a famous novel — nothing beyond your reading position, unless you explicitly ask to be spoiled.
External links — the About panel, the what's-new door — actually open your browser now.
A pasted API key is refused without being echoed back into the conversation.
Book cards can no longer be presented twice in one reply.

entries.summary: A release about PDFs, and about the reader chrome knowing when to get out of the way. A PDF page is a picture, so the page color never reached it and every fixed-layout book stayed on white paper inside a dark app — that is fixed, along with the controls those books were offering but could not honor.

items.title: PDFs follow the page color
items.body: A light palette tints the paper as the page is drawn, leaving every ink and photograph exactly as printed. A dark palette redraws the page in two tones, so the text stays readable instead of sitting as black ink on a dark sheet.

items.title: Page Rendering
items.body: Keep a book on its original colors while everything else follows your palette. Remembered per book, for the art and photography where the color is the point.

Fixed-layout books no longer offer typography they cannot honor. A PDF or comic is a sequence of pages someone else already typeset, so font, size, weight, spacing, alignment and margins are gone for those books. Page color and reading mode stay, because both still do visible work.

The reader toolbar no longer flashes up and vanishes a moment after you tap the page. Anything that re-flows the text — the soft keyboard, rotating the device, changing the font size — was being mistaken for a page turn.
The chat composer takes the caret when you open the panel, not every time the toolbar reappears. On a phone that had been throwing the keyboard over a page you only meant to glance at.

entries.summary: The release where the app stops being a fixed set of features and becomes something you extend. Plugins run in real sandboxes, contribute to almost every surface, and ship through a marketplace. The agent grows tools and traces, the reader grows an ending, and both the book and the conversation are now yours to typeset.

items.title: Plugins
items.body: A full plugin system: sandboxed workers with permission-gated capabilities, a TypeScript-first authoring path, and a marketplace with install-time consent. Plugins contribute reader menus, headers, command-palette entries, whole pages, AI tools, dictionary lookups, themes and bundled fonts, voice engines, scheduled tasks, and even virtual books that live on your shelf like any other title. Five ship built in — Dictionary, RSS Reader, Sentence Reader, TTS Voices, and Editorial Themes.

items.title: Read-aloud
items.body: The reader speaks, following the same sentence and paragraph navigator you read by. Any TTS engine can plug in, with per-provider voices and custom endpoints.

items.title: An ending
items.body: Finishing a book now lands on an end-of-book screen instead of a dead stop, with an optional look back written by the agent.

items.title: Agent as a destination
items.body: The agent gets its own primary page with multiple threads, grounding in where you actually are in the book, expandable execution traces, and tools that can safely read and change your settings.

items.title: More formats
items.body: CBZ, CBR, TXT, and HTML join EPUB, MOBI, AZW3, FB2, and PDF. Covers and metadata fill in at import.

items.title: Make it yours
items.body: Primary navigation and every menu surface are drag-arrangeable. The command palette works while reading, and Mod+1..9 jumps between destinations.

items.title: Typography for the app, not just the book
items.body: Chat replies, notes, and plugin views get their own font, size, and line spacing — following your reading settings by default, or detached if you'd rather. Text alignment becomes a reading setting too, defaulting to whatever the publisher chose.
The progress bar in the reader header is a scrubber you can drag.
Fixed-layout books (PDF, comics) take annotations and swipe page turns.
AI provider setup is simpler, remembers a model per provider, and supports per-tier thinking effort for smart and fast models.
Your API key is encrypted at rest, and AI requests route through native HTTP instead of the webview.
All state changes are event-sourced: projections rebuild from an append-only log and can be verified against it.
The shelf grid fills wide windows, and book titles from file names come out clean.
The desktop app inherits your macOS system proxy.
Dev builds get their own identity and data directory, so they no longer share the release app's library.
Docs and blog on readaware.app are now available in English, Simplified Chinese, and Japanese.
Books whose stylesheets pin a near-black text color are no longer invisible on the dark page color — a whole class of calibre-converted EPUBs was unreadable in dark mode.
EPUB 3 inline footnote bodies stay hidden and open in a popover, instead of dumping a chapter's worth of notes into the prose.
The line-spacing setting now works on books that declare their own line height on paragraphs, where it previously did nothing at all.
Chapter headings in real-world .txt files are recognized.
Android ships with its built-in plugins, and serves plugin assets over the scheme it actually uses.
The marketplace remembers the last mirror that worked.
Stray taps on the reader's progress bar no longer seek on touch devices.
Plugin pages scroll as pages, virtual rows re-measure when content above them changes, and open settings forms adopt external writes instead of shadowing them.
Marketplace file paths are allowlist-validated, closing a Windows drive-relative path bypass.

lake-baikal.title: Lake Baikal: sync that had to be earned
lake-baikal.description: Why 0.5.0 took the longest quiet stretch this project has had: end-to-end encrypted sync, ghost books, an error-handling reckoning, and a wall that was one array long.
lake-baikal.body:
Six weeks ago, in the post about why your library lives on your device, we made a quiet promise: "Sync, eventually." Version 0.5.0 — Lake Baikal — is that eventually. It took eighteen days without a stable release, which is the longest this project has ever gone quiet, and the gap deserves an explanation.

## Why sync is the hard promise

For a normal app, sync is a feature. For a local-first app, it is a test of everything you claimed to believe.

We had committed to two things that make sync brutally unforgiving. First, your data is end-to-end encrypted: the relay server stores ciphertext sealed with a key derived from your passphrase, and nothing else. That sounds like a bullet point until you realize what it costs — the server can never merge your data, never repair it, never even look at it to help you debug. Every hard problem must be solved on your devices, by construction.

Second, ReadAware's storage is an append-only event log; the tables the app reads are projections rebuilt from it. So the unit of sync is not "your books table" — it is every event that ever happened, in an order that must converge no matter which device wrote what while offline. Getting a second device to replay your whole reading life and arrive at the same library is less like copying files and more like proving a theorem about your own past.

So Lake Baikal took the slow road: hybrid logical clocks for ordering, batched replay so a big backlog rebuilds projections once instead of once per page, chunked uploads so a 200 MB scanned book travels in resumable pieces, sign-in that opens the app from a browser link, and a live push channel so a highlight made on your desktop is on your phone before you pick it up. Even your preferences roam — themes, typography, AI settings, API keys — so a fresh install feels like yours in a minute.

## The ghost books

The first real two-device run produced our favorite bug of the release: books that existed on the new device as covers with no pages. Ghosts.

It turned out to be three separate failures stacked so neatly that each one hid the next. The bootstrap copied manifest rows for files whose bytes had never finished uploading. The webview's security policy silently blocked the app from reaching the relay on one platform. And when the relay refused a file for being over the free tier's size cap, the refusal was recorded — silently — in a column nothing displayed. Three quiet failures, one spooky symptom, days of forensics.

The fix was partly code and partly philosophy: sync now has a per-book panel that shows exactly what has and hasn't reached the cloud, and why. A system allowed to fail silently will; the only cure is making its state visible.

## The audit the ghosts demanded

That "silently recorded refusal" bothered us enough that, once sync stabilized, we audited error handling across the entire app. The findings were humbling: fourteen places showed users raw internal errors, eight places swallowed failures a user deserved to know about, and one migration path could quietly delete data after a failed import.

Lake Baikal ships the rebuild: every failure now carries a stable code, surfaces as a localized, actionable message — never a stack trace — distinguishes "empty" from "broken", and offers retry only when retrying can honestly help. And if the app ever crashes, the next launch offers (asks — never auto-sends) a diagnostics report.

## The wall that was one array long

A user reported that Android couldn't import TXT files. We were confused: TXT support shipped months ago. Both things were true. The format support lived in the app; the wall lived in a hardcoded list of MIME types handed to Android's system file picker, written before TXT support existed and never updated. Every .txt file on every Android device was being greyed out by six lines of configuration.

It is the most instructive bug of the release: a feature is not what the code can do, it is what a user can reach. We now test the reach.

## What else is in the lake

The book memory got dramatically faster — the character and concept graph that used to build over hours of idle time now races you, building in the first minutes after you open a book, and the assistant queries it like a tool instead of having it stapled to every prompt. There are two update channels now (Beta, if you like the fast lane), a real OpenRouter model picker with prices, plugins that can theme the whole app and update themselves with rollback, and page turns on the mouse wheel.

Sync ships with a free tier, and paid plans raise the storage when your library outgrows it — that, plainly, is what funds the relay.

Lake Baikal holds a fifth of the world's fresh water, unfrozen under a meter of ice, and has quietly kept everything ever given to it. That felt like the right name for the release where your library learned to survive anything happening to any one device. The lake is deep. Toss your books in.

plugins-v1.title: Plugins: the reader, extended
plugins-v1.description: ReadAware now has a plugin system and a community marketplace. Selection actions, native-looking pages, agent tools, and books that aren't files.
plugins-v1.body:
ReadAware now has a plugin system. You can write a plugin in an evening, install it from a folder while you develop it, and submit it to a community marketplace where anyone can install it in one click.

## What you can build

A plugin is a folder with a manifest and one JavaScript module, and it can contribute:

- **Selection actions** — select text in any book and act on it: send a word to Anki, translate a passage, post a quote to your notes app.
- **Header buttons and pages** — a popover on the reader's top bar, or a full page on the shelf.
- **Commands** — everything lands in the command palette automatically.
- **Tools for the assistant** — this is the one we care most about. A plugin can hand the reading agent a new tool, and the agent decides when to call it mid-conversation. "Which of these words are already in my Anki deck?" becomes answerable.
- **Books that aren't files** — a content provider serves chapters on demand, so an RSS feed can sit on your shelf and be read, highlighted, and discussed exactly like a book.

## Native by construction

We took the interface philosophy from Raycast: plugins do not render their own UI. They declare views — markdown, lists, forms, structured blocks — and the app renders them with its own design system. A plugin page is indistinguishable from a built-in one, because it is built from the same parts. Plugin authors do zero design work; the app stays one calm surface.

And you stay in charge of the furniture: plugins contribute capabilities, but Settings → Menus decides which buttons appear where, in what order. New plugin actions arrive in the overflow menu, not in your face.

## Honest about trust

The trust model is Obsidian's, stated plainly: plugins run inside the app, and installing one is trusting its author. Manifests declare permissions — network, reading data, AI, clipboard — and the API enforces them, which catches accidents, not malice. So the app shows you every permission in plain language before a single file is copied, and the marketplace reviews every submission in the open, readable source required. No dark corners, no "it's sandboxed" theater.

## Start here

The [API reference](/docs/plugins/api) documents the whole contract, and the [marketplace repository](https://github.com/ahpxex/readaware-plugins) has a TypeScript template plus the official plugins as working examples. Write one, and when it is good, [send it in](/docs/plugins/publishing) — the marketplace tab in Settings is waiting for its first community plugins.

local-first.title: Your library is not a cloud feature
local-first.description: Why ReadAware keeps your books, annotations, and memory on your device, and what the network is actually for.
local-first.body:
ReadAware stores your books, your annotations, and the memory it builds about your reading on your device. Not cached locally with a cloud copy as the real one — stored, as the source of truth, in a local database the app reads and writes directly.

This is unusual enough for a modern app that it deserves an explanation, because it is not an implementation detail. It is the design.

## A reading app knows too much

A library is one of the more intimate datasets a person has. What you read, what you underline, what you ask about a difficult passage at 1 a.m. — an app that watches you read holds something closer to a diary than to a media collection.

ReadAware's whole premise makes this sharper. The product is memory: it distills your highlights and conversations into a durable profile of what you read and how you think. Building that and then shipping it to someone else's server by default seemed, to put it mildly, like the wrong trade. So the rule is simple: the data lives with you, and the app must be fully usable offline. Import, read, annotate, search — none of it touches a network.

## What the network is for

Two things, both optional:

- **Inference.** The assistant runs on an API key you bring. Requests go from your machine to your provider — OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, a local-network endpoint, whoever you chose. There is no ReadAware server in the middle, which also means nobody to meter you, upsell you, or log your questions.
- **Sync, eventually.** Multi-device sync is coming, and its design follows the same rule: the server is a dumb relay for end-to-end encrypted change logs. Your devices reconcile; the server stores ciphertext it cannot read. Since there is no server-side feature that needs your plaintext, there is nothing to trade away.

## The quiet benefits

Privacy is the argument that fits in a sentence, but daily life with a local-first app is mostly about other things. Everything is fast, because every read is a local read. Nothing spins. The app works on a plane, in a dead zone, and in ten years — if we disappeared tomorrow, your library and every note in it still open on your machine, and your books are still the original files you imported.

Software you rely on for thinking should be structured like something you own, not something you rent. This one is.

reading-that-remembers.title: Reading that remembers
reading-that-remembers.description: ReadAware 0.1 is out. Why we built another reading app: highlights that go somewhere, and an assistant with a memory.
reading-that-remembers.body:
ReadAware 0.1 is out today, for macOS, Windows, and Linux. It is a reading app — another one — and this post is about why we thought the world needed it anyway.

## Highlights go nowhere

Every serious reader we know has the same ritual. You read, you mark the passages that matter, and the marks accumulate somewhere you will honestly never look again. The highlight was the point of contact — the moment a book actually changed what you were thinking — and the software treats it as an archive entry.

The AI chat era made this stranger, not better. You can now paste a chapter into a chatbot and have a genuinely good conversation about it. But the conversation evaporates. Next book, next chat, blank slate. The assistant that discussed Meditations with you last month has no idea it ever happened.

## Memory, not transcripts

ReadAware is built around one idea: the unit of intelligence in a reading app is not the book, it is your reading — the trail of highlights, notes, questions, and conversations you leave across books. So the app is designed memory-first:

- Every book has one continuous conversation. You never manage chat threads inside a book; you just keep talking.
- The assistant does not reread an ever-growing transcript. What matters is distilled into durable memory — what you are reading, what you asked, what you keep coming back to — and recalled when it is relevant.
- Your highlights and notes are not an archive. They are material the assistant actually works from.

Ask "how does this connect to the last book I read?" and that question makes sense here. That is the product.

## One reader, every format

The mundane half of the product had to be right, too. EPUB, MOBI, AZW3, FB2, and PDF all open in the same reader with the same selection, annotation, and progress model. Nothing is converted — the file you import is the file you keep. DRM-locked files are the one thing we cannot open.

## Yours, on your machine

Your library, annotations, and the memory the app builds all live on your device. AI runs on a key you bring, talking directly to your provider. There is no account and no server reading your books. More on this in a coming post — it is a deliberate architecture, not a temporary state.

ReadAware is free, and it is young — 0.1 means 0.1. If you read seriously and want your reading to accumulate into something, [install it](/docs/install) and tell us what breaks.
